title: Mahatma Gandhi and Lord Reading: Satyagraha Meets Imperial Diplomacy — 1921
summary: In May 1921, Viceroy Lord Reading held six historic private interviews with Mahatma Gandhi, discovering that pure moral candor is far more disarming than cunning diplomacy.
keywords: Historical Dialogue 137: காந்தியும் மை கறை பட்ட புடவையும்: “கங்கை, யமுனை சேர்ந்துவிட்டன!”
full_text:
In May 1921, the newly appointed Viceroy of India, Lord Reading—a former Lord Chief Justice of England celebrated for his formidable legal intellect—invited Mahatma Gandhi to the Viceregal Lodge in Simla.

The Non-Cooperation Movement was sweeping the subcontinent. Reading intended to cross-examine Gandhi as he would an adversary in court, probing for political inconsistencies, hidden ambitions, and legal vulnerabilities.

Over six days of exhaustive, hours-long personal interviews, Gandhi sat serenely in his coarse khadi shawl, answering every probing question with absolute transparency. He had no secret files, no political leverage to conceal, and no tactical deception.

Following their final interview, Lord Reading wrote a candid, astonished letter to his son in England:
"There is something in him that baffles ordinary diplomatic judgment. He does not converse like a typical political leader. He is transparent to the point of impossibility. When I ask him what his next step will be, he tells me plainly, without fear or calculation, exactly how he intends to bring our administration to a standstill through non-violent non-cooperation! As a judge, I know how to break a cunning liar or expose an intrigue. But against a man who conceals nothing and speaks only what he believes to be absolute moral truth, our traditional statecraft feels utterly powerless."

Gandhi demonstrated that unyielding adherence to truth is the ultimate weapon against imperial subterfuge.
